newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway central bank warns economy may overheat.
newsitem.headline: Norway central bank warns economy may overheat.

text.p: Norwegian central bank governor Kjell Storvik on Wednesday revised the 1997 inflation forecast upwards and warned politicians the booming economy was heading towards overheating.
The central bank projected consumer price inflation at between 2.75 percent and 3.0 percent this year, up from 2.5 percent in a similar inflation report three months ago.

Giving a range rather than its customary target, the bank said the projection depended on movements in the exchange rate of the crown, which has rallied recently on the back of the oil-driven Norwegian economy.

Overall gross domestic product (GDP) growth for 1997 was upgraded to 4.25 percent from 3.5 percent three months ago. It was seen at 3.25 percent next year to continue an economic upturn begun in 1994.
Mainland GDP, which excludes the thriving offshore oil and gas sector, was projected to grow 3.25 percent this year, up from 3.0 percent in the previous report.
Private consumption was seen to grow by 4.0 percent, up from 3.5 percent.

"We are of course concerned with the development in the Norwegian economy at present because, as you say, we are heading towards a situation of overheating," Storvik said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).
Asked if the upwards revision of inflation forecasts for 1997 meant the economy was indeed overheating now, he said:

"Not at present. We have upgraded our inflation estimate also because there have been tax increases which go into the CPI figures in Norway and there has been a fairly strong increase in electricity prices due to the weather conditions in Norway."
John Eriksen, an analyst with I.D.E.A., a financial research institution in London, said he was surprised the inflation forecast was revised upwards.
"I would have lowered it because import prices have dropped as a result of the strong crown, and the statistics office in February forecast 1.8 percent for 1997.

"This illustrates a great uncertainty in the Norwegian inflation outlook. Key issues will be the impact of import prices and whether strong domestic demand actually will manifest itself in higher consumer prices," Eriksen said.
Storvik said the inflation outlook now depended partly on the outcome of wage negotiations in the labour market.

He said the central bank would have preferred a tighter fiscal policy than the one adopted in the government budget in December and said it was up to politicians to secure stability in the economic development.

The central bank's deposit rate, which constitutes the floor for money market rates, has been cut by some 150 basis points since March 1996 in fruitless attempts to keep the petroleum currency from appreciating.

"There is hardly any doubt that the sharp fall in interest rates through 1996 and 1997, in conjunction with marked wage growth, are some of the factors behind the brisk growth in consumption," Storvik said.

A survey by the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development said on Monday that Norway's strategy -- with monetary policy focussing on exchange rate stability and fiscal policy geared to inflation control -- was coming under strain now that the risk of inflationary tensions was rising.
OECD said a restrictive monetary policy was now necessary.
Storvik rejected the advice, saying: "I think OECD is not observing the total economic policy stance in Norway."
